Question two. What is overfitting, and how do you combat it? It's a model that has memorized its training data: low training error, high validation error. Learning curves show it. On a standard benchmark with ten inputs, five of them noise, an unpruned tree has zero training error at every size, and its validation error is still falling at two thousand rows. The gap is variance, and a gap still closing says more data will help. So get more data, cut capacity, regularize with L one, L two or dropout, augment the data, or stop early. Question three. What is underfitting? Both errors high, and close together. A straight line on the same data has two curves that meet within a few hundred rows, both near seven, and more rows won't move them. It needs more capacity, longer training, less regularization, or better features. Add a product of two inputs and a square, and its error falls from six point nine to four point six.

Question four. L one versus L two regularization? Both add a penalty on the weights to the loss. They differ in what happens to a small weight. The page's run has twenty features, five of them informative. Ridge, the L two penalty, keeps all twenty: the useless ones shrink below a quarter, but none reaches zero. Lasso, the L one penalty, keeps exactly the five. L two pulls in proportion to the weight, so the pull fades as the weight shrinks. L one pulls just as hard all the way down, so a weight that isn't earning its keep lands on zero. In production that's a saving: five features to compute at serving time, not twenty. With correlated features, lasso keeps one arbitrarily, and elastic net, which mixes both penalties, keeps the group. Every fix so far was judged on validation data. Next, how to keep that judgement honest.
